extraction.name: CoNLL-2003 named entity data
extraction.description: A named entity recognition dataset covering English and German, with eight files: training, development, test, and unannotated data for each language. Annotated entities belong to four categories: persons, locations, organizations, and miscellaneous names. The unannotated files contain 17 million English tokens and 14 million German tokens.
extraction.citeAs: Erik F. Tjong Kim Sang and Fien De Meulder. Introduction to the CoNLL-2003 Shared Task: Language-Independent Named Entity Recognition. arXiv:cs/0306050v1, 12 June 2003.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: English texts were selected from the Reuters Corpus. Ten days of news stories from the end of August 1996 were used for training and development, December 1996 stories for testing, and September 1996 stories for the unannotated data. German texts were extracted from the Frankfurter Rundshau newspaper portion of the ECI Multilingual Text Corpus. Articles from one week at the end of August 1992 were used for training, development, and testing; articles from September through December 1992 supplied the unannotated data.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis; Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: English Reuters news stories from the Reuters Corpus, which covers August 1996 through August 1997; German newspaper articles from Frankfurter Rundshau in the ECI Multilingual Text Corpus.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Data were divided into separate training, development, test, and unannotated files for each language. The separation of development and test data was chosen to avoid tuning systems to the test data. Files contain one word per line, with empty lines marking sentence boundaries. Annotated lines contain the word, part-of-speech tag, chunk tag, and named entity tag.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: All raw data were processed with a tokenizer, part-of-speech tagger, and chunker. Two basic language-specific tokenizers were created for the shared task. English data were tagged and chunked with the memory-based MBT tagger. German data were lemmatized, tagged, and chunked with the decision-tree tagger Treetagger.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: English and German training, development, and test data were manually annotated for named entities at the University of Antwerp, mostly following MUC conventions. Labels distinguish persons (PER), organizations (ORG), locations (LOC), and miscellaneous names (MISC). MISC includes names outside the other categories, including adjectives such as Italian and events such as 1000 Lakes Rally. The IOB scheme uses O for words outside entities, I-XXX for words inside an entity of type XXX, and B-XXX for the first word of an entity immediately following another entity of the same type. Entities are assumed to be non-recursive and non-overlapping; usually only the top-level entity is annotated when entities are nested.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Named entity annotation was performed at the University of Antwerp.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: MBT, a memory-based tagger, for English part-of-speech tagging and chunking; Treetagger, a decision-tree tagger, for German lemmatization, part-of-speech tagging, and chunking.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The texts contain names of persons and locations, which are annotated as PER and LOC. The dataset contains English and German text.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Named entities are represented as non-recursive and non-overlapping; when an entity is embedded in another entity, usually only the top-level entity is annotated. The MISC category is described as very diverse. The linked data files are available without the words.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Developing and evaluating machine-learning systems for language-independent named entity recognition. Training files are used to train models, development files to tune parameters, and test files to compare system performance without tuning to the test data. The shared task encourages incorporating unannotated data and external resources such as gazetteers into learning. Evaluation uses entity-level F1, with an entity counted as correct only when it exactly matches the corresponding annotated entity.
